description_short: Bhante Bodhidhamma explores the hindrance of dullness and lethargy (thīna-middha), its causes, how it differs from depression, and practical methods to overcome it in meditation and daily life.
description_long:
In this practical talk, Bhante Bodhidhamma addresses thīna-middha — dullness and lethargy — one of the five hindrances that obstruct meditation progress. He notes that while sensual desire and ill-will receive much attention, this particular hindrance is often underestimated despite being remarkably pernicious in its effects on our practice and daily attitude.

Bhante explains the Pāli terminology: thīna refers to dullness in the mind while middha indicates physical heaviness or torpor. He traces how this hindrance develops through habitual patterns — the comfortable lingering in bed, the retreat to the sofa when bored or upset, creating what he evocatively calls 'a sort of soft suicide' that generates downward-pulling energy. He shares the striking observation from the Burmese Arahant Sunlun, who achieved liberation with remarkable speed and attributed most practitioners' slower progress simply to laziness.

Drawing on the Buddha's advice to Venerable Moggallāna, Bhante offers numerous practical antidotes: changing the meditation focus, pulling the earlobes, opening the eyes to let in light, walking meditation, and mindful rest when all else fails. He carefully distinguishes between the temporary state of drowsiness — which responds to energising techniques — and clinical depression, which is a persistent trait requiring different support. The talk includes guidance on investigating the quality of dullness itself as a meditation object, sometimes resulting in sudden awakening 'like a light bulb.'

Bhante concludes with memorable reflections on impermanence and urgency as motivators, and the observation that dullness and restlessness are often two expressions of the same energy — one rising, one falling — offering a technique of scanning upward from the feet to lift sluggish energy.
